result: Deep cortical stimulation elicits a triphasic spiking pattern (brief excitation, off period, rebound excitation) in both cortex and thalamus during wakefulness. Thalamic bursting is necessary for the late EEG component, and cortico-thalamo-cortical interactions drive the long-lasting evoked EEG signals. This pattern is reduced during running and absent during anesthesia.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this as a major finding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'makes a fundamental observation about the role of activity in the mouse thalamus on scalp recorded voltage fluctuations' with 'compelling support.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'the conclusions regarding the thalamic contributions to the ERP components are strongly supported by the data' and identifies 'showing the contribution of thalamic activity to some components of the cortical ERP' as 'the most important point of the paper.'

result: Cortical stimulation elicits a widespread, complex ERP with two prominent peaks (at ~25 ms and ~180 ms) during wakefulness when stimulating deep layers, but a simpler ERP with only the early component when stimulating superficial layers. Deep stimulation produces significantly longer duration and larger magnitude ERPs compared to superficial stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 2 affirm the approach is 'novel' and results are 'compelling' and 'convincing.' Reviewer 3 states 'the study is very well performed' with 'appropriate methodology' and that 'the conclusions...are strongly supported by the data.' No reviewer questions these basic ERP characterization findings.

result: Superficial stimulation evokes local responses with minimal spread to other areas, while deep stimulation evokes widespread LFP, CSD, and spiking responses across multiple cortical regions. About three times more cortical neurons respond significantly to deep than to superficial stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the data 'seemingly contradicts the results presented in Histed et al. (2009)' and states 'it is clear that the maximum effect happens near the electrodes, decays with distance, and it is not sparse at all,' offering 'proof that microstimulation might be much more effective than it was thought.' This indicates the reviewer accepts and validates these findings as significant.

result: Thalamic neurons are almost eight times more likely to be modulated by deep than superficial stimulation. During the initial excitation, cortex precedes thalamus by ~7 ms, but during rebound excitation, thalamus precedes cortex by ~36 ms. Deep stimulation significantly increases the likelihood of evoking thalamic bursts.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the conclusions regarding the thalamic contributions to the ERP components are strongly supported by the data.' The timing relationships and burst findings are central to the main conclusion about thalamo-cortical interactions, which all reviewers accept.

result: A pronounced current sink in deep cortical layers coincides with thalamic rebound burst timing (~180 ms). The fraction of bursting thalamic neurons correlates with cortical population firing rate and with the magnitude of the late ERP component. EEG signals correlate more strongly with deep layer CSD than superficial layer CSD.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the 'sophisticated analysis of neural signals provides compelling support' for the observations. Reviewer 3 states the study shows 'convincing evidence' for thalamic contributions to ERP. These correlation analyses directly support the main mechanistic claim, which reviewers accept.

result: Behavioral state modulates evoked responses: the late ERP component is diminished during running and absent during anesthesia. Baseline firing rates are higher during running and lower during anesthesia. Thalamic burst probability decreases during running and is very low during anesthesia. Thalamic activity precedes cortical activity during rebound in both quiet and active wakefulness.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the effects of behavioral state on brain responses to stimulation are generally convincing.' All reviewers accept the state-dependent findings without challenge, treating them as well-supported observations.

result: PCIST (perturbational complexity index) is higher during awake than anesthetized states in all subjects. PCIST is significantly lower for superficial than deep stimulation. PCIST is highest during quiet wakefulness, lower during active wakefulness, and lowest during anesthesia. PCIST recovers to pre-anesthesia levels within 30 minutes after cessation of isoflurane.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that 'the spatiotemporal complexity is almost a side point' but does not challenge the validity of these measurements. Reviewers 1 and 2 describe the results as 'compelling' and 'convincing' without raising concerns about the PCI analysis.

result: During initial excitation, the fraction of activated neurons is always higher in stimulated cortex than other areas. In the off period, very few neurons show increased spiking, but many show decreased spiking. All subjects receiving deep stimulation showed significant rebound excitation in stimulated cortex, whereas only 1/6 superficial stimulation subjects did.
evaluation: These detailed single-neuron analyses support the main findings about triphasic patterns and are part of the 'sophisticated analysis' that Reviewer 1 notes provides 'compelling support.' No reviewer questions these characterizations.

result: The authors provide mechanistic interpretations of the observed patterns, including that superficial stimulation produces a biphasic pattern reminiscent of bistability in unconscious states, while deep stimulation produces a triphasic pattern. They propose mechanisms involving cortical down-states, thalamic hyperpolarization, and low-threshold Ca2+ spikes.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these mechanistic interpretations as reasonable inferences from the data. Reviewer 3 explicitly validates the findings by noting they contradict Histed 2009 and provide evidence that 'microstimulation might be much more effective than it was thought,' indicating acceptance of the proposed mechanisms.

result: The authors discuss that thalamic relay neurons exhibit evoked rebound bursting during quiet wakefulness but not during running or isoflurane anesthesia, consistent with prior literature showing state-dependent thalamic bursting and isoflurane's effects on low-threshold Ca2+ spikes.
evaluation: These claims integrate the current findings with prior literature. Reviewer 2 states the behavioral state effects are 'generally convincing,' and no reviewer challenges these interpretations or their consistency with prior work.

result: The authors characterize baseline firing rates across states and link stimulus-evoked thalamic bursts to longer, higher amplitude ERPs, consistent with prior studies showing thalamic bursts robustly activate cortical neurons.
evaluation: These supporting analyses are part of the overall characterization that reviewers find compelling. Reviewer 1 notes the 'sophisticated analysis' and Reviewer 2 finds the state effects 'convincing.'

result: The authors report that PCIST values are higher during awake than anesthetized states, with an inverted-U relationship suggesting an optimal network state for complexity in mice, reminiscent of arousal-performance relationships.
evaluation: While Reviewer 3 notes complexity is 'almost a side point,' no reviewer challenges the validity of these PCI findings. The interpretation about optimal network states is presented as an inference consistent with prior work.

result: The authors discuss qualitative differences between mouse and human ERPs, noting that the two prominent components seen in mice are not apparent in human TMS-evoked EEG. They attribute this to anatomical differences, including more layer 2/3 neurons in primates and more layer 5/6 neurons in mice, consistent with their findings of pronounced cortico-thalamic activation in mice.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these comparative discussions. The authors acknowledge limitations while maintaining that the study provides 'novel and unexpected results linking the ERP to activity in the CTC loop,' which reviewers accept.

result: The authors discuss methodological differences between electrical stimulation and TMS, noting that electrical stimulation directly activates axons while TMS acts mainly trans-synaptically. They note similarities with human studies showing suppression of high frequencies (off periods) near stimulation sites.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly validates the effectiveness of electrical microstimulation, stating the data 'seemingly contradicts' Histed 2009 and shows microstimulation is 'much more effective than it was thought.' This supports the authors' methodological approach.

result: The authors provide extensive background on PCI as a technique for assessing consciousness, reviewing prior human and rodent studies. They note that none of the previous rodent studies simultaneously recorded micro- and macro-signals (neurons, LFP, and EEG).
evaluation: This background material establishes context and is not challenged by reviewers. The claim about simultaneous multi-scale recording being novel is implicitly accepted as it motivates the study design that reviewers find compelling.

result: The authors describe their experimental setup including a 30-electrode EEG array and biphasic current pulses (200 μs/phase, 10-100 μA). They note that the first ERP peak amplitude decays with distance and flips sign (likely volume conduction), while the second component changes differently, suggesting different mechanistic origins.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a methodological concern about the average reference montage potentially removing useful signal components, especially during anesthesia: 'it is possible...that under isoflurane anesthesia, electrical stimulation induces a generalized slow wave or a burst of activity across the brain. Subtracting the average signal will simply remove that from all channels.' This suggests uncertainty about whether the EEG analysis fully captures the evoked responses, particularly in the anesthetized state.

result: The authors discuss implications for consciousness research, noting that their findings of shorter, less complex ERPs and reduced CTC circuit effectiveness during anesthesia are compatible with studies on neuronal correlates of consciousness. They conclude the study provides novel results linking ERPs to CTC loop activity and opens doors for future causal studies.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these broader implications. Reviewer 1 states the work 'will likely be of broad interest to neuroscientists,' and Reviewer 3 emphasizes this as showing 'convincing evidence to the contrary' of the view that 'scalp ERP's have long been regarded as purely cortical phenomena.'
